item.title: Black Sea: Development and Reconstruction for Regions Facing Disruptions
item.content:encoded:
Courtney Bower, Cornell University

This special issue invites empirically grounded research examining how the Black Sea region recovers and transforms amid conflict, economic transitions, and geopolitical uncertainty. The editors welcome submissions employing quantitative methods such as econometrics, input-output modeling, GIS, remote sensing, network analysis, and agent-based models, as well as mixed methods approaches. Studies offering actionable policy recommendations for diverse stakeholders including municipalities, port authorities, government ministries, and international organizations are particularly valued.

Appel publié par Growth and Change. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Spatial configurations and governance arrangements for resilient recovery
  • Corridors, gateways, and supply chains under geopolitical stress
  • Cross-national comparisons of economic, institutional, and geopolitical trajectories
  • The Black Sea as a complex adaptive system
  • Multi-scalar analyses of infrastructure networks
  • Displacement, migration, return, and relocation
  • Energy security and vulnerability in contested sub-regions
  • Regional development transitions: past, present, and future
  • Urban–rural disparities and interdependencies
  • National and regional innovation systems and spillovers
  • Diaspora finance and development
  • Cross-scale policymaking shaping growth trajectories
  • Workforce development, skills matching, and labor-market recovery
  • Roles of institutional actors, international organizations, and non-governmental entities

Timeline

  • September 30, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Social Wellbeing, Human Health and Location
item.content:encoded:
Konstantinos Eleftheriou, University of Piraeus

Peter Nijkamp, University of Rijeka

Konstantinos Christopoulos, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

This special issue investigates how geographic location influences wellbeing and health outcomes for individuals and communities. While social science research increasingly employs quantitative methods to measure wellbeing factors and health determinants, the spatial dimension has often been overlooked. The issue recognizes that geography profoundly shapes how people experience wellbeing and health, contributing to significant regional and urban disparities across developed and developing countries.

The special issue welcomes empirical studies examining the quantitative relationships between wellbeing, health, and location at both urban and regional scales. Research should employ solid theoretical frameworks and applied quantitative methodologies, with particular interest in policy-oriented studies that identify geographic drivers of unequal wellbeing and health outcomes.

Appel publié par Growth and Change. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • geographical determinants of wellbeing and health
  • impacts of climate change and human adaptivity
  • human-environmental interfaces and livability
  • lifestyle, food security and quality of life
  • healthcare access and human happiness
  • socio-economic inequality effects on lifestyle and behaviour
  • access to urban green and life satisfaction
  • spatially discriminating implications of public health policy
  • mobility, transportation and sustainable city life
  • impacts of water scarcity and quality on human quality of life
  • spatial health spillovers (e.g. infectious diseases)

Timeline

  • November 30, 2026: Submission deadline
